[TEST] Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE)

[THOUGHT]  
This is a classic presentation of sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) in a young, otherwise healthy male during intense physical exertion — a hallmark red flag for inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy. The absence of prodromal symptoms, unremarkable personal/family history, and normal baseline ECG (aside from LVH voltage criteria) initially obscure the diagnosis, but the echocardiogram revealing **asymmetric septal hypertrophy** is pathognomonic for **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)** — the most common cause of SCA in young athletes. While other entities (e.g., arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, Wolff-Parkinson-White, coronary artery anomalies) must be considered, none are supported by the available evidence: no ECG repolarization abnormalities, no structural RV disease on echo, no preexcitation, and no family history suggestive of channelopathy. The exertional trigger, lack of acute ischemic markers (though troponin pending), and absence of coronary disease on angiography (expected to be normal) further solidify HCM as the substrate. Importantly, SCA in HCM often occurs *without* prior symptoms — up to 30–40% of first presentations are sudden death or resuscitated arrest. The confirmed structural abnormality + SCA event meets definitive diagnostic criteria for HCM per ACC/AHA/ESC guidelines and establishes it as the underlying etiology — not just an association.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
